draft.title: Water use in the Murray-Darling Basin
card: The Murray-Darling Basin is Australia's largest river system. It covers a large part of inland south-eastern Australia and crosses several states and the ACT.
The basin grows much of Australia's food. Irrigation, which means watering crops with water taken from rivers, is the biggest use of its water.
Towns and cities along the rivers also take water for drinking, homes and industry. Some towns rely on the rivers for most of their supply.
The rivers and wetlands need water too, to keep plants, animals and water quality healthy. Every drop taken out leaves less in the river, so the water must be shared between these uses.
draft.remember: The basin's water is shared between irrigation, towns and the rivers themselves.

a.q: Why must the water of the Murray-Darling Basin be shared?
opts: Farms, towns and rivers all use it, and taking some leaves less
Only farms need water, so towns must wait for what is left
The rivers are too small to supply any farms or towns
Each state owns its own river, so none can be shared
a.why: Irrigation, towns and the rivers themselves all depend on the same water, and taking some leaves less for the others. The idea that only farms need it is wrong, because towns and the rivers need water too.
a.clue: Think about who uses the water, and what happens when one user takes more.

b.q: Sam grows cotton beside a river in the basin and takes water from it to irrigate his crop. Which use of basin water is this?
opts: Irrigation for farming
Water supply for a town
Water left for the river environment
Water used in a dam for flood control
b.why: Taking river water to water crops is irrigation, the biggest use of water in the basin. It is not left in the river, so it is not water for the environment.
b.clue: What is Sam using the water to do?

wants.brief: A map of the Murray-Darling Basin showing its extent across inland south-eastern Australia, with the states it crosses (Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia) and the ACT, and its main rivers, the Murray and the Darling.
wants.why: Students see how large the basin is and that it crosses several states, which is why its water must be shared.
notes: At 360 px the map's legend, town names, source line and credit block are far too small to read, so most of its labels cannot be read on a phone; a simpler map with only the basin, the states, the ACT and the main rivers would suit the card.
The card and the request name the ACT, but the map does not label it: only a tiny Canberra dot inside a faint dashed border shows it.
The map adds a Murrumbidgee label that the card never mentions, and a miles scale an Australian student does not need.

The Commons file is not the MDBA's map as published: a Commons user (SCHolar44) added the state and river names and the scale bars, as the line under the map says, so the record should credit those changes and not only 'Resized and compressed'.
The Commons page's attribution note says the Government of South Australia owns the copyright, which contradicts the MDBA as creator, so who to credit is not clear from the page.

At the width the app draws it on a 360 px phone (about 296 px, so the 500 px map shrinks to about 0.6), the city names, the legend and the Australian Capital Territory label come out at roughly 6 to 8 px and are too small to read.

The whole map is used, including the Northern Territory, most of Queensland and Tasmania, which the card does not need; cropping to the basin and the states it crosses would make the labels about half as large again.
The Australian Capital Territory and Victoria labels sit across river and state boundary lines, and the Canberra dot sits on a tributary, which makes them harder to read once the map is shrunk.

figures.alt: A map of the Murray-Darling Basin. The basin covers a large part of inland south-eastern Australia: southern Queensland, much of New South Wales, northern Victoria, the ACT around Canberra, and the east of South Australia. The Darling River runs south-west across New South Wales to join the Murray, which flows west to the sea in South Australia.
